full_text_en:
Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation v. Beijing Cultural and Art Publishing House Audio-Visual World — copyright infringement dispute

Plaintiff: Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation, domiciled at 229 South State Street, Dover, Kent County, Delaware, United States of America.

Representative: Mary Anne Harrison, Senior Vice President.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Yongyi and Zhang Bin, lawyers of Beijing Dadi Law Firm.

Defendant: Beijing Cultural and Art Publishing House Audio-Visual World, domiciled at No. 114 West Chang'an Avenue, Xicheng District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Pan Hongye, General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Li Dazhong, lawyer of Beijing Long An Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Li Hao, copyright agent of Beijing Copyright Agency.

The plaintiff, Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Fox), filed a lawsuit with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court against the defendant, Beijing Cultural and Art Publishing House Audio-Visual World (hereinafter referred to as the Audio-Visual World), for copyright infringement.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The plaintiff is the lawful owner of the copyrights in the cinematographic works "COMMANDO" and "DIE HARD 1, 2". Pursuant to the "Memorandum of Understanding on the Protection of Intellectual Property Rights" signed between the Chinese Government and the United States Government on January 17, 1992, and the provisions of the "Berne Convention" which entered into force for China on October 15, 1992, the copyrights owned by the plaintiff in the said cinematographic works shall be protected under the "Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China". Prior to the initiation of this lawsuit, the plaintiff had never authorized the defendant to distribute or sell the plaintiff's cinematographic works, nor had it authorized any third party to license the defendant to do the same. The plaintiff discovered that recently, without authorization, the defendant had distributed and sold laser discs of cinematographic works whose copyrights are owned by the plaintiff. The defendant's use of the works by means of video recording, distribution, etc., without the plaintiff's permission, constitutes a serious infringement of the plaintiff's copyrights and should bear the corresponding legal liability for infringement. Therefore, the plaintiff requests the People's Court to: 1. Order the defendant to provide the sales quantity and inventory quantity of the infringing products; 2. Seize and confiscate all unsold infringing products of the defendant; 3. Order the defendant to provide a written guarantee to the plaintiff that it will not infringe the plaintiff's copyrights in the future; 4. Order the defendant to pay the plaintiff compensation of no less than RMB 50,000; 5. Order the defendant to bear the expenses incurred by the plaintiff in pursuing the defendant's liability for infringement.

Defendant's Defense: (1) The cinematographic work publications involved in this case were published and distributed by Shenzhen Laser Program Publishing and Distribution Company. This fact is clearly marked on the products. The plaintiff's allegations are inconsistent with the facts. (2) China's Copyright Law stipulates that only using cinematographic works by means of video recording constitutes infringement. The Copyright Law does not stipulate that those who distribute or sell on commission infringing publication products that cannot be clearly identified should bear liability for infringement; nor does it stipulate that those who distribute or sell on commission publication products must obtain permission from the copyright owner. Article 46(2) of the Copyright Law states: "Without the permission of the copyright owner, reproducing and distributing his works for profit" is an infringement. Therefore, only providing copies of a work without authorization for a specific purpose constitutes an illegal act of distribution. A distributor can achieve the purpose of distribution by directly providing copies of the work to the public through its own sale or rental, or indirectly providing copies of the work to the public through marketing channels such as sale or rental. A marketer of publications is not necessarily a publisher or distributor. The plaintiff's accusation that the defendant "used the works by means of video recording" is a misinterpretation of the law. The plaintiff has no legal basis to assert rights against the defendant, who is not a publisher or distributor. (3) The defendant is merely a consignment seller of the publications involved in this case and cannot state the full sales situation of the said publications to the court. The plaintiff should be clear about the publication, distribution, and marketing situation of the said publications and should assert rights against the unauthorized user of the works. The plaintiff, solely because the Audio-Visual World is the largest-scale and most influential audio and video product marketing enterprise in Beijing, has made the Audio-Visual World the sole defendant and arbitrarily expanded the content of its claims. Its litigation motive is improper and should not be supported.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found the following facts upon trial: The plaintiff, Fox, is a film company incorporated in the United States. Fox registered copyrights for its cinematographic works "COMMANDO" (1985) and "DIE HARD 2" (1990) with the U.S. Copyright Office and obtained copyright registration certificates, thus owning the copyrights in the said cinematographic works.

On June 6, 1994, the plaintiff's lawyer purchased laser discs of "COMMANDO" and "DIE HARD 2" published and distributed by Shenzhen Laser Program Publishing and Distribution Company from the defendant, the Audio-Visual World. The plaintiff's said purchase was preserved as evidence by the Beijing Notary Public Office through notarization. The defendant raised no objection to the accusation of its sales and the notarization by the Beijing Notary Public Office. The certificate issued by Shenzhen Laser Program Publishing and Distribution Company submitted by the defendant shows that "DIE HARD" was approved for publication by Document No. 118 (1989) of the Ministry of Culture, and "COMMANDO" was approved for publication by Document No. 200 (1990) of the Ministry of Culture. The defendant also submitted an Import Publication License for Overseas Literary and Artistic Audio-Visual Products, the content of which does not involve the cinematographic works in this case.

The defendant, the Audio-Visual World, is a legally established enterprise legal person, with its business scope including audio-visual products that are officially published and distributed by the state. The defendant failed to provide corresponding evidence to prove the consignment sales relationship it claimed to have with Shenzhen Laser Program Publishing and Distribution Company.

In November 1995, upon the plaintiff's application, the court preserved the accounts of the defendant, the Audio-Visual World, as evidence and commissioned an auditing firm to audit the sales of the relevant laser discs by the Audio-Visual World. The audit conclusion was: during the period from October 16, 1993 to October 31, 1995, the Audio-Visual World's sales were as follows: (1) "COMMANDO": purchases amounting to RMB 4,589.76; sales of 20 discs amounting to RMB 5,993.40; one disc in stock amounting to RMB 218.56; profit of RMB 806.40; (2) "DIE HARD": purchases of 32 discs amounting to RMB 6,539.04; sales of 22 discs amounting to RMB 5,603.40; 10 discs in stock amounting to RMB 1,987.20; profit of RMB 469.04.

The plaintiff's opinion on the audit report was: The operating expenses of the defendant in selling infringing products are related to the infringing act; therefore, operating expenses should not be deducted from the sales revenue, and the gross profit from sales should be regarded as its illegal income. That is, the illegal income should be the balance after deducting sales cost (purchase price) and taxes from the sales revenue.

The defendant did not submit its opinion on this audit report.

During the trial, the plaintiff clearly stated that, because it did not know whether the production date of the laser discs sold by the defendant was after the effective date of the Sino-US "Memorandum of Understanding on the Protection of Intellectual Property Rights", it would temporarily not sue the producer and publisher of the laser discs. This lawsuit only targets the seller.

The expenses incurred by the plaintiff for this lawsuit include: (1) The cost of purchasing the laser discs sold by the defendant to obtain evidence: RMB 350.30 for "COMMANDO", RMB 350.30 × 2 = RMB 700.60 for "DIE HARD 2", totaling RMB 1,050.90. (2) The notarization fee for evidence preservation to collect evidence: RMB 562.50. (3) The notarization fee for the bilingual Chinese-English consistency of litigation documents: RMB 600. (4) The translation fee paid to the translation company for the translation of litigation documents: RMB 638.75. (5) Lawyer's agency fee: RMB 4,662.41. The total above is RMB 7,514.56.

The plaintiff also claimed that the defendant should compensate for the prepaid case acceptance fee and prepaid audit fee, totaling over RMB 19,000.

The above facts are confirmed by the following evidence: the plaintiff Fox's registration certificate, copyright registration certificates for the cinematographic works "COMMANDO" and "DIE HARD 2", the Notarial Certificate of Evidence Preservation No. 1219 of Beijing Notary Public Office, the laser discs "COMMANDO" and "DIE HARD 2" sold by the Audio-Visual World, the audit report, fee receipts, the business license of the Audio-Visual World, the publication approval explanation, the Import Publication License for Overseas Literary and Artistic Audio-Visual Products, the consignment sales explanation, and statements of the parties.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held: The defendant, the Audio-Visual World, sold laser discs produced based on the cinematographic works "COMMANDO" and "DIE HARD 2", for which the plaintiff Fox enjoys copyright. The reproduction of these laser discs was done without the permission of the copyright owner; therefore, the said laser discs sold by the Audio-Visual World are infringing products. This is the main fact of the case. The focus of the dispute between the parties is: whether the sales conduct of the Audio-Visual World constitutes an infringement of Fox's copyrights? This shall be determined in accordance with the Copyright Law and international copyright treaties:

From a subjective perspective, the defendant, the Audio-Visual World, was at fault in selling the infringing laser discs. The defendant's main argument that its conduct does not constitute infringement is that it has no obligation to examine the copyright legality of the laser discs it distributes. Document No. 28 (1993) of the National Copyright Administration, "Notice on the Specific Copies of Foreign Works Used for Specific Purposes", stipulates that before the international copyright treaties take effect in China, specific copies of foreign works owned and used by Chinese citizens or legal persons for specific purposes must obtain authorization from the original copyright owner to be sold after October 15, 1993; otherwise, it will be treated as infringement. Sellers of audio-visual products must not only comply with industry management regulations but also pay attention to whether the audio-visual products they sell may infringe upon the intellectual property rights of others. After China acceded to relevant international copyright conventions and treaties, sellers should be even more cautious in their business operations concerning foreign works protected by Chinese law. The defendant, as a professional seller of audio-visual products, failed to pay attention to whether the laser discs it sold were infringing goods and continued to sell them without obtaining authorization from the original copyright owner, thus being subjectively at fault. Its excuse for exemption from liability, that the laser discs it sold were official publications provided by a third party, cannot be established. From an objective perspective, as China and the United States signed the "Memorandum of Understanding on the Protection of Intellectual Property Rights" and China acceded to the "Berne Convention", the copyrights obtained by the plaintiff Fox in the United States for the cinematographic works "COMMANDO" and "DIE HARD 2" should also be protected by Chinese law. Article 5(5) of the "Regulations for the Implementation of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China" stipulates: "Distribution means providing a certain number of copies of a work to the public through sale, rental, etc., to satisfy the reasonable needs of the public." Therefore, sale is also a distribution act under the Copyright Law. Article 45(5) of the "Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China" stipulates: "Using a work by means of performance, broadcast, exhibition, distribution, filming of cinematographic works, television, video recording, or adaptation, translation, annotation, editing, etc., without the permission of the copyright owner" is an infringement. The defendant, by selling infringing laser discs published by others in Beijing, infringed upon the plaintiff's legitimate rights and interests and shall bear corresponding legal liability. Of course, after bearing the liability, the seller may seek recourse from the publisher pursuant to the contract.

Although the laser discs sold by the defendant, the Audio-Visual World, bear approval numbers from the cultural administrative department, these approval numbers were all granted before the "Memorandum of Understanding on the Protection of Intellectual Property Rights" and the "Berne Convention" became effective in China, at which time the department did not examine copyright licensing issues. The defendant failed to provide evidence that the sale of the laser discs had obtained copyright permission; therefore, it cannot be exempt from liability. The Import Publication License for Overseas Literary and Artistic Audio-Visual Products submitted by the Audio-Visual World does not relate to the cinematographic works in this case and is therefore irrelevant to this case and cannot be used as a defense evidence. The defendant's claim that its relationship with the publisher, Shenzhen Laser Program Publishing and Distribution Company, is one of consignment sales cannot be accepted due to lack of corresponding evidence. Moreover, according to the law, regardless of whether the relationship between the parties is consignment sales or purchase and sale, it does not affect the assumption of legal liability for infringement towards a third party.

In considering the damages for infringement, regard should be given to the time during which the defendant, the Audio-Visual World, carried out the infringing act, the quantity of infringing products sold, the consequences of the damage caused by the sale of infringing products, and the social impact caused by the infringement. The plaintiff's opinion that operating expenses should not be deducted from the profit on the sale of infringing products is reasonable and should be adopted. Therefore, the plaintiff's loss can be calculated based on the reasonable profit the plaintiff should have earned per disc and the quantity of infringing products sold by the defendant. The reasonable expenses of RMB 7,514.56 incurred by the plaintiff in seeking judicial relief to protect its legitimate rights and interests shall also be borne by the defendant.

The plaintiff's claims that do not fall within the scope of civil judgment, such as ordering the defendant to provide a written guarantee of non-infringement, are not supported by the court.

Accordingly, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on November 26, 1996: (1) The defendant, Beijing Cultural and Art Publishing House Audio-Visual World, shall immediately cease the sale of laser discs that infringe the copyrights of the plaintiff, Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation.

(2) The defendant, Beijing Cultural and Art Publishing House Audio-Visual World, shall pay compensation of RMB 20,114.56 to the plaintiff, Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation, within 30 days from the effective date of this judgment.

(3) The remaining claims of the plaintiff, Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation, are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 2,010, the audit fee of RMB 10,000, and other litigation costs of RMB 125 shall be borne by the defendant, Beijing Cultural and Art Publishing House Audio-Visual World.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court also, in accordance with the provisions of Article 134(3) of the "General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China", separately issued a Civil Sanction Decision to confiscate the infringing laser discs in stock at the defendant, Beijing Cultural and Art Publishing House Audio-Visual World.

After the first instance judgment was pronounced, neither party filed an appeal.
